newsitem.title: FRANCE: Hopes high ahead of annual Burgundy wine auction.
newsitem.headline: Hopes high ahead of annual Burgundy wine auction.

text.p: Nursing high hopes for the 1996 vintage, wine lovers from around the world poured in to the Burgundy wine capital of Beaune on Saturday for the annual Hospices de Beaune charity auction.

The Sunday event, ending three days of feasting and drinking in the wine-dependent region, is closely watched by wine professionals and drinkers as the earliest public assessment of this year's vintage.
In a country whose third biggest export is wine, the auction is also closely watched as an indicator of the trade's health.

Attention is expected to be intense this year as the auction will be first since an international outcry last year over Paris's nuclear testing programme, which triggered an informal boycott of French products around the world.
Burgundy's wine board last month expressed optimism about the new vintage, saying the harvest held great promise.

"The grapes, in red as in white, were of good quality with high levels of sugar, good acidity, sustained colour for red wines and were in an exceptional state of health," the board said in a recent news release.

The harvest under good weather conditions resulted in a 27 percent increase in the quantity of wine to be auctioned, the wine board said. It said 719 casks would be sold, 607 of red and 112 of white wines.

Proceeds from the sale after production costs go to Beaune's charity hospital, founded in 1443. Over the last several hundred years the hospital has been given about 61 hectares (150.7 acres) of vineyards spread over 38 of France's finest cuvees.
The wines on sale at the annual event include such international superstars as Montrachet, Pommard, Corton, Vougeot and Volnay, and often fetch more than $2 million under the hammer.

The auction, which dates from 1859, will this year be carried live on the internet for the first time. A page on the world wide web, hosted by four journalists, will be updated each 15 minutes with prices and developments.
Tastings of the young wine, still stored in oak barrels, were being held at several sites around Beaune.
The young wine must age in huge oak barrels before it can be bottled and put on sale, a process that takes several years with the most prestigious wines.

Beaune's centre was bustling ahead of the auction, with flags hanging from building fronts and the steets filled with well-dressed foreigners. Busy shopkeepers tried to make the most of the flood of tourists, wine professionals and journalists.
Prices at last year's auction rose 7.8 percent from 1994 when they soared by just over 50 percent after several years of declines. The Hospices was hoping for another price increase this year.
"It's a great year for chardonnay grapes," those used in Burgundy's white wines, spokeswoman Annie Ligen told Reuters.
